thought: I start with a small range [2, 5,000] where every witness can be checked exactly with rational arithmetic.  A correct baseline is a precondition for trusting any later scaling.
observation: 4,999 witnesses verified; 75 first-step failures; first failures [49, 73, 169, 193, 241, 313].

thought: The simplest possible law is that the greedy step never fails.  Even a five-thousand-point scan is enough to test it.
observation: H0 is refuted: n=49 needs k=2; there are 75 failures in this small range.

thought: I do not want to guess a modulus.  I build a generic feature library (residue classes and 'all prime factors in a residue class' predicates, for both n and the first greedy denominator x0), then run a beam search for the simplest zero-false-positive conjunction.
A rule that fits 50k points may be an artefact.  I test it on a twenty-times larger range and count every false positive and false negative.

The failures are not spread uniformly over residues.  The two-literal rule forces n ≡ 1 (mod 12): n must be 1 mod 4, 1 mod 3, and share the 3-smooth condition with (n+3)/4.  I tabulate the empirical density to make that visible.
observation: residues with at least one failure: [1]; residue 1 carries 11.3% failures, all other residues 0.

thought: With a theorem candidate in hand I can afford a much larger scan.  The precondition is that the step test is a finite abelian-group computation, not a search over denominators.
observation: scan finished in 24.7s; distribution top = [(13, 1), (14, 4), (15, 5), (27, 1)]; last record n=8803369, k=27.

thought: The full-range audit is the strongest finite check I can make in this campaign.  It is not a proof, but it rules out a hidden counterexample up to the scan limit.

A record is only interesting if I can explain why the greedy step failed so many times.  For each record I extract a certificate: at step j the reachable divisor residues form a proper subset of (Z/pZ)*, and -1 lies outside it.
observation: last record n=8,803,369: k=27, chain length 27, witness z≈3.294e+15 (z/n²=42.501).

thought: The step test is a divisor-residue criterion, not the original definition.  I close that gap with an independent brute-force search over all admissible denominators for a small range.
Existence and height are different questions.  The greedy witness is the first solution it can certify, not the shortest one.  I measure how far the certified height can drift above n² and n³.
observation: max z/n²=1.492e+08 at n=767,761; max z/n³=194.3 at n=767,761; 13 cases with z>n³.

thought: The height spikes are not random.  At step j=5 the modulus is p=19.  If n ≡ 9 (mod 19) then q = n x₅ ≡ n²/4 ≡ -13 (mod 19), and if n ≡ 33 (mod 52) then 13 divides x₅.  Hence d=13 is admissible, and because it is small the certified height is ≈ q²/(19·13) ≈ n⁴/(16·19·13).
The records are not evenly spaced.  I fit the maximal index against ln N and check whether a two-parameter logarithmic law is a reasonable first description.
A single logarithmic line fits poorly.  I compare three two-parameter laws: linear in ln N, a power of ln N, and a power of N.  With seven prefix points the comparison is descriptive, not asymptotic.
I now check the cross-cutting conjectures that emerged from the scans: record holders being prime, the logarithmic growth of k_max, and the behaviour of the height ratio.
The campaign is complete.  I freeze the trace, the certificates and the figures, and state the surviving hypotheses and the open questions.
